notes: Implements the global option correctly: repeated options append, names go to the automate loader with no route, it works with no site blocks, internal names get the internal issuer, and existing site-block policies are respected without a conflicting duplicate. Global ACME defaults apply through a base policy that consolidation folds back in, and the hasGlobalACMEDefaults extraction is a justified refactor. Policy matching is exact-subject only (wildcard site-block policies are not considered), and the comments are verbose; five adapt tests cover the main scenarios well.

The option parses correctly and appends when repeated. Names go into the automate loader with no route, and public names get a global-options-derived policy that consolidation folds back into the same shape a dummy site block would produce. Non-public names go to the internal issuer, and names that already have a site-block policy keep that policy, so no conflicting policy is created. The refactor into a hasGlobalACMEDefaults helper is small and justified, and five adapt tests cover the main scenarios (no site block, auto_https off, existing policy, internal names, repeated option). Comments are somewhat verbose, and subject matching is exact-string only, which is the minor edge-case gap.

The new exact `hreflect.CompareNumbers` (int, uint and float mixes; NaN, ±Inf and the 2^63/2^64 bounds) is correct and is wired consistently into `Eq`, `compareGet` and `Where`, but the patch also changes the shared `ConvertIfPossible` helper: it stops dereferencing pointers and refuses lossy float conversions, and it rewrites existing tests to bless that, which risks regressions for other callers and goes beyond the issue, as does the large unrelated benchmark.

The new hreflect.CompareNumbers helper compares int, uint and float values exactly and is wired into eq/ne, compareGet and where, so the core fix is correct and well tested. However, the patch also changes the shared ConvertIfPossible helper: it no longer dereferences pointers, float conversions are now lossless-only, and existing tests were rewritten to match. It also adds a large unrelated benchmark and refactors Comparer handling, all beyond scope. Where now passes numeric results through int64 as a hack, and NaN `!=` in where returns false where it used to return true.
